Use this process for any new entry in the Hosted API model catalog, including:
- New upstream model families (e.g., Llama, Qwen, Mistral)
- New sizes or instruction variants
- New upstream releases that change tokenizer, weights, or license

# Roles
- Requester: typically Product or Solutions Engineering
- Intake owner: Applied ML Onboarding (Applied ML)
- Runtime owner: Serving Runtime
- Release owner: Release Engineering
- Security gate owner: Security & Compliance
- Docs owner: DevEx / Docs

# Intake ticket and required fields
Create a Linear ticket in *ENG* with label `model-onboarding` and include the following fields (copy/paste section):

## 1) Model identity
- Upstream model name and version tag
- Model type: `chat` | `completion` | `embeddings` | `rerank`
- Upstream repo / source URL
- Tokenizer type and expected special tokens

## 2) Intended catalog surface
- Proposed Redwood model ID (e.g., `rw/llama-3.1-70b-instruct`)
- Compatibility target: `redwood` native | OpenAI-compatible endpoint
- Any planned aliases (e.g., `rw/llama-3.1-70b`)

## 3) License and redistribution
- License name + link to full text
- Redistributable weights: yes/no/unclear
- Any use restrictions that must be enforced in ToS / UI (e.g., geo, user class)

## 4) Data and policy
- Safety/policy concerns (e.g., uncensored, adult content)
- Any known PII or training data controversies (link sources)

# Intake gates (must all be satisfied to proceed)
1. **License pre-check** (Owner: Finance-Legal liaison + Security)
 - Outcome: `approved`, `approved w/ restrictions`, or `blocked`
 - Artifact: link to Security risk review page entry (see Security space)
2. **Baseline evaluation plan** (Owner: Applied ML)
 - Outcome: evaluation suites selected + success criteria

- Artifact: eval plan comment in Linear + link to eval harness run(s)
3. **Feasibility / runtime fit** (Owner: Serving Runtime)
 - Confirm tokenizer handling, KV cache behavior, and kernel coverage
 - Artifact: short feasibility note + any required runtime flags

# Artifacts produced during intake (and where they live)
- Model intake summary: Linear ticket (single source of truth)
- Eval plan + results: Eval harness run links and Confluence (Applied ML and Evals)
- Performance benchmark results: Confluence Performance Standards page + attached benchmark run IDs
- Quantization plan/results: Confluence Quantization Profiles space

- Security risk review: Confluence Security & Compliance space
- Rollout plan and fallback: Confluence Eng Platform runbook
- Model registry change: GitHub PR in `redwood-model-registry`

# Definition of “ready for implementation”
A model is ready to move from intake to implementation when all of the following are true:
- License is approved (or approved with documented restrictions)
- Eval plan includes at least one internal prompt set and one public benchmark
- Runtime owner has stated no known blockers
- A rollout owner is named (release + platform)

Summary
-------
This playbook describes a repeatable process for converting observed runtime workload signatures into defensible Service Level Objectives (SLOs) and cost-sensitivity profiles for Redwood inference services. It ties together sampling, profiling, experiment design, and SLO derivation so teams can make consistent, evidence-based SLOs for new routes, model variants, and capacity plans.

Scope
-----
Applies to: all inference-facing HTTP/streaming routes and internal RPCs that contribute to model-serving latency or cost. Excludes: purely offline batch jobs (see eng-infra runbooks) and human-in-the-loop lab experiments.

Definitions
-----------
- Workload signature: a compact description of request shape and distribution (sequence length percentiles, batching patterns, KV cache hit ratio, request concurrency, special flags like streaming or tool-calls).
- Cost-sensitivity: the change in per-request GPU/time cost when a workload attribute shifts (e.g., +10 tokens => +X ms / +Y token-cost).
- SLO bucket: a named target (e.g., P95 latency 120ms for interactive, P99 500ms for high-throughput) tailored for a workload class.

Key Principles
--------------
- Evidence-first: SLOs must be justified by sampled production telemetry and controlled experiments.
- Workload-driven segmentation: avoid one-size-fits-all SLOs; segment by signature clusters that materially change cost/latency.

- Cost-aware guardrails: every SLO must include an associated cost-sensitivity statement used for tradeoff decisions (e.g., whether to enable larger batch sizes or fallback to cheaper model variants).
- Operational observability: each derived SLO must have dashboards, automated alerts, and an attached experiment plan for periodic revalidation.

references.text:
Summary
-------
This playbook describes a repeatable process for converting observed runtime workload signatures into defensible Service Level Objectives (SLOs) and cost-sensitivity profiles for Redwood inference services. It ties together sampling, profiling, experiment design, and SLO derivation so teams can make consistent, evidence-based SLOs for new routes, model variants, and capacity plans.

Scope
-----
Applies to: all inference-facing HTTP/streaming routes and internal RPCs that contribute to model-serving latency or cost. Excludes: purely offline batch jobs (see eng-infra runbooks) and human-in-the-loop lab experiments.

Definitions
-----------
- Workload signature: a compact description of request shape and distribution (sequence length percentiles, batching patterns, KV cache hit ratio, request concurrency, special flags like streaming or tool-calls).
- Cost-sensitivity: the change in per-request GPU/time cost when a workload attribute shifts (e.g., +10 tokens => +X ms / +Y token-cost).
- SLO bucket: a named target (e.g., P95 latency 120ms for interactive, P99 500ms for high-throughput) tailored for a workload class.

Key Principles
--------------
- Evidence-first: SLOs must be justified by sampled production telemetry and controlled experiments.
- Workload-driven segmentation: avoid one-size-fits-all SLOs; segment by signature clusters that materially change cost/latency.

- Cost-aware guardrails: every SLO must include an associated cost-sensitivity statement used for tradeoff decisions (e.g., whether to enable larger batch sizes or fallback to cheaper model variants).
- Operational observability: each derived SLO must have dashboards, automated alerts, and an attached experiment plan for periodic revalidation.

Purpose
This document (Ops Orchestra) defines the canonical, company-wide procedures for access and permissions, change management, data classification & handling, procurement and expenses, vendor onboarding & management, travel policy, and a small library of standard templates. It is intended for managers, approvers, and people-ops/finance partners who execute or govern cross-functional
operational processes.

Scope
Applies to all Redwood Inference employees, contractors, and vendors that require platform, finance, or HR-related access or services. Exceptions must be approved by the relevant owner_team and logged in the change registry.

Owners and SLAs
- Document owner: finance-legal
- Primary operational leads: Security (access changes), Eng-SRE (infrastructure change runs), Finance (procurement/expenses), People-Ops (travel & benefits)
- Target SLA for routine approvals: 72 business hours
- Emergency/expedited approvals: same-day (see Emergency change section)

1) Access & Permissions
1.1. Access model
- Roles: Employee, Contractor, Service (machine identity), Admin
- Principle of least privilege (PoLP) is required for all roles. Role permissions must be justified in the access request ticket.
- Temporary access: granted using time-bound roles (max 14 days for privileged work).

1.2. Request and approval flow
1. Submit access request via internal access-portal (link: /internal/tools/access-portal). Include: owner, justification, resources, duration, and approver group.
2. Security review: Security reviews high-scope requests (production, key stores, billing).
3. Grant: System auto-provisions where templates exist; otherwise manual provisioning by Cloud Ops within SLA.
4. Verification: Requester confirms access; owner_team marks request closed.

- Standard change: low-risk, pre-approved templates, no downtime (automated).

- Membership: Eng-SRE, Platform, Security, Product, and one Finance/Legal representative.

- Title

- Type (standard/normal/emergency)
- Rollout window & maintenance window
- Backout/rollback plan
- Canary/verification steps and SLOs to observe
- Impacted services and customers

2.4. Deployment checklist (example)
1. Create change ticket in change-registry (link: /internal/tools/change-registry).
2. Attach runbook and rollback commands.
3. Confirm tests in staging and smoke tests.
4. Schedule and notify stakeholders 48 hours before the window.
5. Execute canary rollout; monitor latency/error metrics for 30 minutes.

Purpose
This document (Ops Orchestra) defines the canonical, company-wide procedures for access and permissions, change management, data classification & handling, procurement and expenses, vendor onboarding & management, travel policy, and a small library of standard templates. It is intended for managers, approvers, and people-ops/finance partners who execute or govern cross-functional
operational processes.

Scope
Applies to all Redwood Inference employees, contractors, and vendors that require platform, finance, or HR-related access or services. Exceptions must be approved by the relevant owner_team and logged in the change registry.

Owners and SLAs
- Document owner: finance-legal
- Primary operational leads: Security (access changes), Eng-SRE (infrastructure change runs), Finance (procurement/expenses), People-Ops (travel & benefits)
- Target SLA for routine approvals: 72 business hours
- Emergency/expedited approvals: same-day (see Emergency change section)

1) Access & Permissions
1.1. Access model
- Roles: Employee, Contractor, Service (machine identity), Admin
- Principle of least privilege (PoLP) is required for all roles. Role permissions must be justified in the access request ticket.
- Temporary access: granted using time-bound roles (max 14 days for privileged work).

1.2. Request and approval flow
1. Submit access request via internal access-portal (link: /internal/tools/access-portal). Include: owner, justification, resources, duration, and approver group.
2. Security review: Security reviews high-scope requests (production, key stores, billing).
3. Grant: System auto-provisions where templates exist; otherwise manual provisioning by Cloud Ops within SLA.
4. Verification: Requester confirms access; owner_team marks request closed.

references.text: Purpose: This playbook consolidates company-wide procedures for entitlements (access and permissions), change governance, data handling expectations, procurement and expense approvals, vendor lifecycle management, and travel approvals. It is intended for all Redwood employees and contractors who request or approve resources, commit changes to production, or manage third-party relationships.

Scope: Applies to hosted, dedicated, and private deployment teams, platform and infra teams, procurement interactions, people-ops travel arrangements, and any third party that will access Redwood systems or customer data.
Quick links: Access Portal (Okta + Access Request), VendorHub (procurement back-end), ExpenseFlow (employee expenses), Legal intake form, Security questionnaire (security.redwood.local).

Roles and responsibilities
--------------------------

- Requestor: person initiating an access, change, purchase, vendor relationship, or travel booking. Responsible for completeness and business justification.
- Manager/Approver: direct manager who validates business need and budget availability.
- Approving Officer (Finance/Procurement): validates procurement thresholds, tax, and vendor classification.

- Security Reviewer: evaluates data access risk and mandatory controls (SOC2, encryption, contract clauses).
- Legal Reviewer: reviews contract terms for vendor agreements above threshold or with custom IP/data terms.
- Proc Ops (Vendor Onboarding): completes supplier setup, obtains W-9/COI as applicable.

Principles
----------

references.text:
- Least privilege: grant minimal entitlements required for the job and set automatic expiration where practical.
- Segregation of duties: approval and provisioning paths must not be owned by the same individual for medium/high risk requests.
- Evidence-first approvals: all approvals must be attached to the request in VendorHub or Access Portal.
- Risk proportionality: stricter controls for vendors
with data access, privileged infra access, or requests above financial thresholds.

Access & permissions (entitlement lifecycle)
-------------------------------------------
1) Request process

- Use the Access Portal (accessible from the Redwood Console > Tools > Access Request).
- Provide: justification, target systems (service name and environment), requested role (exact RBAC role), duration, and manager approval.
- For long-lived roles (>90 days), supply quarterly business justification and add reviewer in Access Portal.
2) Approval matrix (summary)

- Day-to-day access to non-prod systems: manager approval.
- Prod read-only access: manager + security notification.
- Prod privileged/infra access (SSH, K8s-admin, DB write): manager + security + infra-owner approval.
- Emergency elevated access: break-glass procedure (see Runbook ID: RG-2026-breakglass).
3) Provisioning and deprovisioning

- Provisioning is automated via Okta + Terraform runbooks (Infra-IAC). On approval, provisioning SLA is 2 business days for standard requests, 8 hours for emergency sprints.
- Access expirations are enforced: default 30 days for contractor requests, 90 days for internal hires unless renewed.
4) Periodic review
- Quarterly access attestation: team owners must validate active entitlements and remove stale accounts. Failure to respond triggers automated revocation notices.

The prescribed sequence of actions during a major production outage involves diagnosing and mitigating cross-tenant emergent failures using the Emergent Tenant Behavior Simulation (ETBS) harness and operator playbooks. This includes identifying and addressing issues through observable signals such as resource contention, KV-prefix cache thrashing, and indirect latency spikes. [S1](confluence:dsid_007cbc5fb0fd42a49290950884e2b72a#:~:text=Summary%3A%5CnThis%20runbook%20describes%20the%20Emergent%20Tenant%20Behavior%20Simulation%20%28ETBS%29%20harness%2C%20the%20operator)

> Summary:
This runbook describes the Emergent Tenant Behavior Simulation (ETBS) harness, the operator playbook for diagnosing and mitigating cross-tenant emergent failures, and the dashboards/alerts recommended for early detection. ETBS is a lightweight lab and production-adjacent simulator used to reproduce tenant interactions that cause unexpected resource contention, KV-prefix cache thrashing,

The major production outage is addressed by simulating tenant interactions that cause unexpected resource contention and latency issues, with the goal of reducing time-to-mitigate for hard-to-reproduce degradation patterns. [S2](confluence:dsid_007cbc5fb0fd42a49290950884e2b72a#:~:text=and%20indirect%20latency%20spikes.%20The%20goal%20is%20to%20reduce%20time%2Dto%2Dmitigate%20for%20hard%2Dto%2Dreproduce)

> and indirect latency spikes. The goal is to reduce time-to-mitigate for hard-to-reproduce degradation patterns and to provide prescriptive operator actions tied to observable signals.

Scope:
- Systems covered: LLM inference runtime, KV prefix cache, batching layer, tenant priority queue, regional routing, and serving-side prefetch components.
- Environments: non-prod simulation cluster

The 60 to 90 minutes period is critical for diagnosing and mitigating issues, as the ETBS is used to reproduce tenant interactions that cause unexpected resource contention and latency issues. [S2](confluence:dsid_007cbc5fb0fd42a49290950884e2b72a#:~:text=and%20indirect%20latency%20spikes.%20The%20goal%20is%20to%20reduce%20time%2Dto%2Dmitigate%20for%20hard%2Dto%2Dreproduce)

> and indirect latency spikes. The goal is to reduce time-to-mitigate for hard-to-reproduce degradation patterns and to provide prescriptive operator actions tied to observable signals.

Scope:
- Systems covered: LLM inference runtime, KV prefix cache, batching layer, tenant priority queue, regional routing, and serving-side prefetch components.
- Environments: non-prod simulation cluster

The live coordination call is part of the process to diagnose and mitigate cross-tenant emergent failures, involving notification of customer-success for tenants included in the production-guide. [S3](confluence:dsid_007cbc5fb0fd42a49290950884e2b72a#:~:text=%28primary%29%2C%20canary%20region%2C%20and%20production%20operator%2Dguided%20sandbox.%5Cn%2D%20Not%20covered%3A%20client%2Dside%20application%20bugs%2C)

> (primary), canary region, and production operator-guided sandbox.
- Not covered: client-side application bugs, upstream model weight corruption (separate model-onboarding flow).

Owner and Contacts:
- Runbook owner: Maya Patel (Platform Reliability)
- Primary on-call owner: Platform Operators (eng-platform oncall rotation)
- Secondary escalation: Runtime Team (eng-serving-runtime)
- Pager

Confirming the service is healthy again involves monitoring for improvements in evictions and latency, and promoting to a 30m scheduled policy if certain thresholds are met. references.text:
Severity classification (reference)
1) Sev 0 / Major outage: Global platform unavailability or >50% of regional capacity degraded for >15 minutes.
2) Sev 1 / Partial outage: Major customer-facing functionality down for multiple customers or single large customer impacted for >30 minutes.
3) Sev 2 / Degradation: Latency or errors that materially affect quality but do not block request completion.

SLO thresholds that trigger enterprise evidence path
- Availability SLO: 99.95% monthly. Threshold: If rolling 1-hour availability < 99% for any region -> evidence path.
- Error rate: p99 error rate above 0.5% sustained for 30+ minutes -> evidence path.
- Latency: p99 tail > 3x target latency for >15 minutes for endpoints serving dedicated customers -> evidence path.

Roles and responsibilities
- Incident Commander (IC): Primary decision maker for scope and customer communications. (Example: oncall SRE escalation lead)
- Bridge Lead: Runs the incident bridge, ensures evidence collection tasks are assigned.
- Evidence Custodian: Tracks, stores, and timestamps all artifacts (SRE or Security engineer).

- Customer Success Liaison: Owns customer comms, coordinates legal and account execs.
- Legal / Compliance Contact: Reviews regulatory language and retention/disclosure obligations.
- Postmortem Author: Writes the formal report and ties evidence items to timeline entries.

Status page taxonomy:
- Operational: No customer-facing impact.
- Degraded: Potential for increased latency/cost but no correctness loss.
- Partial outage: measurable customer success/regression for subset.
- Major outage: broad customer impact.
Customer-facing template (Degraded)
Subject: Redwood Inference - Degraded performance for <service> in <region>
Hi <customer-name>,

We are investigating a performance degradation affecting <service> in <region>. During this time, you may experience increased response times or higher-than-normal inference costs. No correctness errors have been observed. Our team has applied temporary routing and throttling to stabilize the service and is actively investigating the root cause.

What we are doing:
- Routing traffic to a lower-memory variant while we investigate
- Temporarily limiting burst capacity for affected tenants where needed
- Performing telemetry analysis and scheduling targeted remediation
Estimated next update: in 60 minutes. If you need immediate assistance, reply to this email or open a support ticket.

Thank you for your patience,
The Redwood Inference Operations Team
Internal status update (Slack announcement example)

[INCIDENT] Maintainability - <service> - Degraded performance (P2)
BC: @<name> | SO: @<name> | RS: @<name>
Summary: Elevated KV cache use causing cost-pressure. Temporary routing to quantized variant applied.
Next update: in 30 minutes.

Content-Type: application/json

args.query: Redwood office adding large planter or wall mounted art approval requirements
parts: Do I need approval to add a large planter or wall mounted art in a Redwood office?
What details should I include in the request?

references.text:
Approval & Ownership:
- Small desk plants and framed prints: no formal approval required.
- Larger items (floor-standing planters, freestanding sculptures, wall-hung installations > 30" in any dimension): submit a short request to people-ops@redwood.com with location, dimensions, weight, and installation method.
- People Ops is the owner for approvals and coordination with building management.

Installation Guidelines:
- Mounting: prefer adhesive strips rated for drywall where appropriate; for heavier fixtures require building-approved anchors and sign-off.
- Electrical: any installation requiring power must be scheduled with facilities and IT; do not run extension cords across walkways.

- Plants: prefer low-allergen, low-light tolerant species for shared spaces (e.g., snake plant, pothos). Avoid high-fragrance plants in kitchens and meeting rooms.
- ID tags: label any communal plant with owner name and watering cadence if not centrally maintained.

Maintenance & Removal:
- Owners are responsible for upkeep. Facilities may remove items that create hazards or persistent nuisances after one week's notice.
- For space reconfigurations, owners will be asked to relocate or remove personal/communal items within two weeks.

Temporary Exhibitions & Events:
- If a team wants to host a temporary exhibit (art show, maker fair, holiday display), submit a proposal at least 10 business days prior including insurance/waiver details if items are valuable.

Quick Checklist (for submitters):
- [ ] Location & footprint
- [ ] Estimated weight
- [ ] Mounting method
- [ ] Owner & contact

references.text: Runtime 1.22 Release Notes — KV Cache Compaction + Tier-Aware Eviction

## Summary
Runtime 1.22 introduces **KV cache compaction** and **tier-aware KV eviction** to reduce GPU memory fragmentation and mitigate burst-driven tail latency (p95/p99) for sustained decode workloads with mixed sequence lengths.

This release adds:
- A **fragmentation-aware allocator health model** (new fragmentation metrics and allocator state tracking).
- **Budgeted compaction** (time/bytes) integrated with the scheduler to avoid decode stalls.
- A **tier-aware eviction policy** (LRU-by-sequence with safety constraints) to prevent opportunistic/chaotic evictions during bursts.

- **Tracing spans and exemplars** to correlate compaction/eviction events with tail latency.
- A **kill-switch** and rollout knobs to allow oncall to disable compaction/eviction quickly.

Primary expected impact:
- Lower tail latency variance during bursts and churn.
- Reduced incidence of “allocator thrash” and fragmentation-driven OOM/forced shedding.
- Minimal steady-state throughput impact when budgets are respected.

## Who is impacted
**Internal:** Runtime, SRE, Release Engineering, Support, Solutions/CS, Product (Hosted + Dedicated).

**External:** Customers on Hosted and Dedicated tiers (and Private if enabled by the account/cluster owner). There are no API surface changes; behavior changes are limited to runtime memory management under load.

## What changed (high-level)
### 1) Compaction (new)
The runtime can now **relocate KV pages** to increase contiguity in the KV arena when fragmentation exceeds a trigger threshold. Compaction is incremental and budgeted to limit latency impact.

references.text:
**Compaction activity**
- `kv_compaction_steps_total` (counter)
- `kv_compaction_bytes_moved_total` (counter)
- `kv_compaction_time_ms_total` (counter)
- `kv_compaction_budget_exhausted_total` (counter) — indicates budgeting is constraining work
- `kv_compaction_stalls_total` (counter) — should be near-zero; investigate if rising

**Eviction activity**
- `kv_evictions_total{reason=pressure|oom_prevent|policy}` (counter)
- `kv_evicted_bytes_total` (counter)
- `kv_evictions_blocked_total{reason=pinned|tier_protected}` (counter) — validates protections

**Latency correlation (golden signals)**
- `runtime_decode_token_latency_ms_p95/p99` (by model, by pool)
- `request_latency_ms_p95/p99` (by route/model)
- Traces: spans `kv.compaction.step` and `kv.eviction.select` (exemplars)

### Typical healthy patterns
- Fragmentation ratio oscillates but returns to baseline after bursts.
- Compaction bytes moved increases during bursts; **compaction time** remains bounded.
- Eviction rate is low/near-zero except under sustained pressure events.

### Red flags
- Fragmentation ratio trending upward with **flat** compaction activity (trigger not met, disabled, or worker stuck).
- High `kv_compaction_time_ms_total` growth accompanied by p99 latency spikes (budget too high or running at bad scheduler phase).

- Sudden increase in `kv_alloc_failures_total` or OOM events while fragmentation is high (eviction not engaging / min-free target too low).
- Non-zero `kv_evictions_blocked_total{reason=pinned}` followed by evictions from pinned sessions (bug / configuration regression).
## Common incidents and how to respond

- `kv.compaction.enabled` (bool)

- `kv.kill_switch` (bool; emergency disable compaction+eviction)

### Recommended defaults (current Runtime 1.22 release train)
Hosted (Shared):
- `kv.compaction.enabled = true`
- `kv.compaction.trigger_fragmentation_ratio = 0.30`
- `kv.compaction.budget_ms_per_step = 2`
- `kv.compaction.budget_bytes_per_step = 268435456` (256 MiB)
- `kv.compaction.max_steps_per_tick = 1`
- `kv.eviction.enabled = true`
- `kv.eviction.policy = tier_aware_lru`

- `kv.eviction.min_free_bytes_target = 1073741824` (1 GiB)
- `kv.kill_switch = false`

Dedicated:
- `kv.compaction.enabled = true`
- `kv.compaction.trigger_fragmentation_ratio = 0.35`
- `kv.compaction.budget_ms_per_step = 3`
- `kv.compaction.budget_bytes_per_step = 402653184` (384 MiB)
- `kv.compaction.max_steps_per_tick = 1`
- `kv.eviction.enabled = true`
- `kv.eviction.policy = tier_aware_lru`
- `kv.eviction.min_free_bytes_target = 536870912` (512 MiB)
- `kv.kill_switch = false`

Private (VPC / On-prem):
- `kv.compaction.enabled = false` (default)
- `kv.eviction.enabled = false` (default)
- If enabling: start with Hosted-like budgets and confirm dashboards/alerts are wired (see Monitoring).

references.text:
This release adds:
- A **fragmentation-aware allocator health model** (new fragmentation metrics and allocator state tracking).
- **Budgeted compaction** (time/bytes) integrated with the scheduler to avoid decode stalls.
- A **tier-aware eviction policy** (LRU-by-sequence with safety constraints) to prevent opportunistic/chaotic evictions during bursts.

- **Tracing spans and exemplars** to correlate compaction/eviction events with tail latency.
- A **kill-switch** and rollout knobs to allow oncall to disable compaction/eviction quickly.

Primary expected impact:
- Lower tail latency variance during bursts and churn.
- Reduced incidence of “allocator thrash” and fragmentation-driven OOM/forced shedding.
- Minimal steady-state throughput impact when budgets are respected.

## Who is impacted
**Internal:** Runtime, SRE, Release Engineering, Support, Solutions/CS, Product (Hosted + Dedicated).

**External:** Customers on Hosted and Dedicated tiers (and Private if enabled by the account/cluster owner). There are no API surface changes; behavior changes are limited to runtime memory management under load.

## What changed (high-level)
### 1) Compaction (new)
The runtime can now **relocate KV pages** to increase contiguity in the KV arena when fragmentation exceeds a trigger threshold. Compaction is incremental and budgeted to limit latency impact.

Key properties:
- **Budgeted per scheduler phase** to avoid decode stalls (see “Default settings by tier”).
- Uses safe stopping conditions; compaction yields when latency-sensitive work is queued.
- Relocation is tracked with counters + traces; correctness is validated under cancellation/churn scenarios.

### Recommended defaults (current Runtime 1.22 release train)
Hosted (Shared):
- `kv.compaction.enabled = true`
- `kv.compaction.trigger_fragmentation_ratio = 0.30`
- `kv.compaction.budget_ms_per_step = 2`
- `kv.compaction.budget_bytes_per_step = 268435456` (256 MiB)
- `kv.compaction.max_steps_per_tick = 1`
- `kv.eviction.enabled = true`
- `kv.eviction.policy = tier_aware_lru`

- `kv.eviction.min_free_bytes_target = 1073741824` (1 GiB)
- `kv.kill_switch = false`

Dedicated:
- `kv.compaction.enabled = true`
- `kv.compaction.trigger_fragmentation_ratio = 0.35`
- `kv.compaction.budget_ms_per_step = 3`
- `kv.compaction.budget_bytes_per_step = 402653184` (384 MiB)
- `kv.compaction.max_steps_per_tick = 1`
- `kv.eviction.enabled = true`
- `kv.eviction.policy = tier_aware_lru`
- `kv.eviction.min_free_bytes_target = 536870912` (512 MiB)
- `kv.kill_switch = false`

Private (VPC / On-prem):
- `kv.compaction.enabled = false` (default)
- `kv.eviction.enabled = false` (default)
- If enabling: start with Hosted-like budgets and confirm dashboards/alerts are wired (see Monitoring).

references.text: ADR-0142: Perf Canary Baselines, Regression Thresholds, Min Sample Sizes, and Anti-Flap Logic

## Status
Published.

## Summary
This ADR defines how the production performance canary computes baselines and evaluates regressions for per-model serving performance (primarily p95 latency and tokens/sec). It documents:
- Baseline computation approach (rolling vs fixed) and when each is used.
- Regression thresholds (warning vs paging) and how they are applied.

- Minimum sample sizes and confidence requirements to avoid noisy alerts.
- Anti-flap / dedupe logic to prevent alert storms during drift, telemetry delays, or small-sample variance.

## Context / Problem
Redwood’s serving runtime changes frequently (kernel selection updates, scheduler heuristics, model config changes, GPU fleet changes, and staged rollouts). We need an always-on canary that:
- Detects real p95 latency regressions and throughput drops early.
- Produces actionable signals for attribution (kernel vs scheduler vs infra).
- Avoids paging on expected variance and baseline drift (e.g., slow fleet mix changes or regional differences).

The key design tension is baseline choice:
- A **fixed baseline** is stable and easy to reason about during rollouts, but can become stale as hardware/driver stacks and workloads evolve.
- A **rolling baseline** adapts over time, but can drift (masking regressions) or create false positives if drift is misinterpreted as regression.

references.text:
## Baseline Computation
### Fixed baseline artifact
- Source: controlled perf-canary runs using the approved synthetic prompt distribution.
- For each baseline key, we store:
 - distribution summaries (p50/p95/p99) for each latency metric
 - mean and standard deviation where stable enough to be meaningful
 - tokens/sec distribution summaries
 - run metadata (time range, sample count, canary config

version)
- Baseline validity: baseline is considered valid only if it meets minimum sample size requirements (see below) and passes sanity checks (no telemetry gaps, no error-rate spikes).

### Rolling health baseline (calibration only)
- Window: trailing 7 days, excluding periods marked as “rollout” or “incident.”
- Aggregation: daily aggregates with robust statistics (median-of-daily-p95) to reduce sensitivity to short spikes.
- Purpose:
 - detect slow drift (e.g., fleet changes) that may warrant generating a new fixed baseline
- suggest region/SKU overrides when variance is consistently higher

## Regression Definition
We define regression as a statistically and operationally meaningful deviation from the fixed baseline.

### Core comparison method (v1)
For each metric M and key K in each evaluation window W:
- Compute observed metric value O(K, W).
- Fetch baseline value B(K) and baseline variability estimates when available.
- Compute percent change: Δ = (O - B) / B.

We use percent change thresholds with guardrails (min samples + sustained breach). Percent thresholds are chosen because:
- Different models have different absolute latencies.
- p95 is the primary SLO-relevant tail metric.

references.text: Postmortem: Perf Canary False-Positive Alert Storm (baseline drift + cardinality)

## Summary
On 2026-02-12, the production performance canary generated a burst of false-positive alerts across multiple models and regions shortly after enabling warning + paging rules in the first expansion beyond the initial 2-model rollout. Alerts were high volume (warning + paging) and repeatedly reopened due to dedupe failures, resulting in on-call interruption and a temporary release freeze
request.

There was **no confirmed customer-facing latency regression** attributable to this incident. The event was an alerting/observability failure caused primarily by (1) **baseline drift + baseline key mismatch** and (2) **metric label cardinality inflation** that fragmented the canary’s time series, defeating min-sample gating and dedupe.

## Impact
### Customer impact

references.text:
The key design tension is baseline choice:
- A **fixed baseline** is stable and easy to reason about during rollouts, but can become stale as hardware/driver stacks and workloads evolve.
- A **rolling baseline** adapts over time, but can drift (masking regressions) or create false positives if drift is misinterpreted as regression.

## Decision Drivers
1. **Low noise / high trust**: warnings should be useful; pages should be rare and high-confidence.
2. **Fast detection**: detect regressions within ~10–30 minutes for top models in covered regions.
3. **Attribution**: baseline keys must align to dimensions needed for root cause (runtime build, kernel tags, SKU).

4. **Operational simplicity**: SRE/on-call should have a predictable interpretation of “regression vs baseline,” including during ongoing rollouts.
5. **Guardrails against drift and telemetry issues**: avoid alert storms caused by baseline drift, delayed metric ingestion, and label cardinality errors.

## Decision
We adopt a **hybrid baseline strategy**:

1) **Primary baseline = Fixed, versioned baseline per (model, model_version, runtime_build, kernel_set_id, hardware_sku) with optional region override**
- Baselines are generated from controlled canary runs (prod-like load) and stored as immutable artifacts.
- Baselines are explicitly tied to the runtime build and kernel selection identifiers so comparisons remain meaningful.
- This is the baseline used for rollout gating and for paging.

references.text:
## What happened (symptoms)
The canary’s regression evaluator compared observed p95 latency/tokens-sec against per-model baselines. After model expansion:
- Many evaluations used **fallback baseline values** because the baseline lookup key did not match (baseline existed under a different dimension set).

- Metric series were fragmented by high-cardinality labels; the regression evaluator saw many “small-N” series and oscillated between “enough samples” and “not enough samples” depending on which series was queried.
- Alert rules did not consistently enforce **minimum sample size across the same grouping** used by the evaluator, which allowed small, noisy slices to trip thresholds.
- incident-bot dedupe keys lacked stable identifiers for (model, version, region, sku, runtime_build), so the same underlying symptom created repeated threads/pages.

## Root cause
### RC1: Baseline drift + key mismatch (primary)
Baselines were stored per (model, runtime_version, hardware_sku, region) in the baseline store, but the canary emitted/evaluated metrics with an expanded set of labels including transient fields and “bucketed” dimensions that were not part of the baseline artifact key.

Specifically:
- The canary evaluation path constructed a baseline key using **(model, model_version, runtime_build, region, hardware_sku, prompt_shape_bucket)**.
- Baseline artifacts were generated for **(model, model_version, runtime_build, region, hardware_sku)** only (no prompt bucket), and in some cases had **region omitted** (older artifacts) because early staging used a simplified schema.
- When the lookup did not match, the evaluator fell back to default thresholds, which are intentionally conservative and therefore easier to breach.

references.text: ADR-0142: Perf Canary Baselines, Regression Thresholds, Min Sample Sizes, and Anti-Flap Logic

## Status
Published.

## Summary
This ADR defines how the production performance canary computes baselines and evaluates regressions for per-model serving performance (primarily p95 latency and tokens/sec). It documents:
- Baseline computation approach (rolling vs fixed) and when each is used.
- Regression thresholds (warning vs paging) and how they are applied.

- Minimum sample sizes and confidence requirements to avoid noisy alerts.
- Anti-flap / dedupe logic to prevent alert storms during drift, telemetry delays, or small-sample variance.

## Context / Problem
Redwood’s serving runtime changes frequently (kernel selection updates, scheduler heuristics, model config changes, GPU fleet changes, and staged rollouts). We need an always-on canary that:
- Detects real p95 latency regressions and throughput drops early.
- Produces actionable signals for attribution (kernel vs scheduler vs infra).
- Avoids paging on expected variance and baseline drift (e.g., slow fleet mix changes or regional differences).

The key design tension is baseline choice:
- A **fixed baseline** is stable and easy to reason about during rollouts, but can become stale as hardware/driver stacks and workloads evolve.
- A **rolling baseline** adapts over time, but can drift (masking regressions) or create false positives if drift is misinterpreted as regression.

references.text:
## Signal object and scoring (product requirements)
### Requirements
- Signals are computed over **daily** and **weekly** windows.
- Each signal includes:
  - Account identifier (org/workspace mapping)
  - Signal type (enum)
  - Window (e.g., last_24h, last_7d)
  - Value + units (e.g., tokens/day, 429_count)
  - Baseline/context (e.g., WoW change)
  - Confidence (low/med/high or numeric 0–100)
  -

Recommended next step (AE/SE/CS action)
  - Dedupe key + version

### Scoring and qualification
- The scoring function outputs:
  - **signal_score (0–100)**
  - **qualification_status**: qualified | suppressed | informational
  - **reason codes** (for auditability)

Initial approach:
- Rule-based scoring for MVP (thresholds + weights by signal type).
- Confidence gates:
  - Minimum volume gate (avoid small-sample false positives)
  - Minimum recurrence gate for intent (avoid single-page “drive-by” views)
  - Internal/test org denylist

### Dedupe and suppression
To minimize spam:
- **Per-account suppression window**: do not create a new HubSpot task for the same signal type within X days unless severity increases materially.
- **Cross-signal suppression**: if an account already has an open task from a “higher priority” signal (e.g., compliance/private intent), suppress lower priority signals for a short period.
- **Marketing touch coordination**: if Marketing nurture is scheduled for the same account segment, suppress or delay AE task creation when appropriate (final rule owned by RevOps + Marketing Ops).

references.text: Audit events for Dedicated rollout actions (staged rollouts)

## Overview
This document defines the audit logging requirements and event schema for **Dedicated staged rollouts for reserved pools**. It covers:
- Event types and semantics for actions: **create/update/promote/abort/hold/force overrides**
- Required fields for compliance, forensic review, and customer change management
- RBAC requirements (who can do what, and what must be logged)

- Retention and export (internal UI + customer export + SIEM)
- Example event payloads
This spec applies to all deployment modes of Dedicated pools (single-region and multi-region), and to all rollout targets (model version, runtime build, routing policy, config changes).

## Goals
1. **Deterministic & auditable change history**: A human reviewer can reconstruct what changed, who initiated it, when it took effect, what gates were evaluated, and why the system promoted/aborted.
2. **Tamper-evident audit trail** suitable for regulated customers’ change-management expectations.
3. **Low risk of sensitive data leakage** (no prompts, user content, or secrets).
4. **Consistent eventing across entry points** (Console, API, automated policy engine actions).

## Non-goals
- Provide a general-purpose eventing framework for all Redwood features.
- Store raw metrics time series in audit logs (we link to evidence queries and dashboards instead).

## Definitions
- **Dedicated pool**: Reserved GPU capacity pool associated with a customer account.
- **Rollout plan**: A staged plan applied to a Dedicated pool.
- **Stage**: A defined traffic/replica partition in the rollout.
- **Gate**: A set of criteria that must pass to promote a stage.
- **Actor**: The entity that initiated the action (human user, service principal, or system automation).

references.text: Postmortem: SEV-2 Console rollout UI bug triggered rollback loop (2026-02-22)

A Console UI change caused repeated client-side retries on a non-idempotent rollback endpoint, putting rollouts-service into a rollback loop for a subset of deployments.
Operators could not reliably pause or promote canary rollouts via Console. Some actions displayed as successful but were not applied, leading to confusion and delayed mitigations for unrelated rollouts.

19:05 UTC: Internal user reported Console rollout controls unresponsive.
19:10 UTC: Eng on-call saw elevated 5xx and increased write QPS to rollouts-service.
19:20 UTC: Isolated to Console release 2026.02.22.2 with a new retry wrapper.
19:28 UTC: Disabled feature flag for retry wrapper in prod.
19:40 UTC: Rollouts-service write QPS returned to normal; rollback loops stopped.

19:58 UTC: Incident resolved.
The Console’s new retry wrapper treated 409 conflict responses as retryable and retried POST /rollback automatically. The endpoint was not idempotent and could re-trigger rollback actions.
Internal report and rollouts-service error/QPS alerts.
Disabled the retry wrapper via feature flag and added a server-side idempotency key requirement for rollback actions.

Feature flag allowed immediate mitigation. Service-level alerts were actionable.
The UI change was not tested against the real rollouts-service conflict behavior; endpoint idempotency was assumed but not documented.
Document idempotency requirements for rollouts-service endpoints (Platform Engineering; due 2026-03-10).

Add integration tests in Console CI that simulate 409 and ensure no retries on non-idempotent endpoints (Console & Tooling; due 2026-03-15).
Introduce a standard client retry policy library with an allowlist of safe endpoints (DevEx; due 2026-04-01).

references.text: Postmortem: SEV-2 Console rollout UI bug triggered rollback loop (2026-02-22)

A Console UI change caused repeated client-side retries on a non-idempotent rollback endpoint, putting rollouts-service into a rollback loop for a subset of deployments.
Operators could not reliably pause or promote canary rollouts via Console. Some actions displayed as successful but were not applied, leading to confusion and delayed mitigations for unrelated rollouts.

19:05 UTC: Internal user reported Console rollout controls unresponsive.
19:10 UTC: Eng on-call saw elevated 5xx and increased write QPS to rollouts-service.
19:20 UTC: Isolated to Console release 2026.02.22.2 with a new retry wrapper.
19:28 UTC: Disabled feature flag for retry wrapper in prod.
19:40 UTC: Rollouts-service write QPS returned to normal; rollback loops stopped.

19:58 UTC: Incident resolved.
The Console’s new retry wrapper treated 409 conflict responses as retryable and retried POST /rollback automatically. The endpoint was not idempotent and could re-trigger rollback actions.
Internal report and rollouts-service error/QPS alerts.
Disabled the retry wrapper via feature flag and added a server-side idempotency key requirement for rollback actions.

Feature flag allowed immediate mitigation. Service-level alerts were actionable.
The UI change was not tested against the real rollouts-service conflict behavior; endpoint idempotency was assumed but not documented.
Document idempotency requirements for rollouts-service endpoints (Platform Engineering; due 2026-03-10).

Add integration tests in Console CI that simulate 409 and ensure no retries on non-idempotent endpoints (Console & Tooling; due 2026-03-15).
Introduce a standard client retry policy library with an allowlist of safe endpoints (DevEx; due 2026-04-01).

references.text: Audit events for Dedicated rollout actions (staged rollouts)

## Overview
This document defines the audit logging requirements and event schema for **Dedicated staged rollouts for reserved pools**. It covers:
- Event types and semantics for actions: **create/update/promote/abort/hold/force overrides**
- Required fields for compliance, forensic review, and customer change management
- RBAC requirements (who can do what, and what must be logged)

- Retention and export (internal UI + customer export + SIEM)
- Example event payloads
This spec applies to all deployment modes of Dedicated pools (single-region and multi-region), and to all rollout targets (model version, runtime build, routing policy, config changes).

## Goals
1. **Deterministic & auditable change history**: A human reviewer can reconstruct what changed, who initiated it, when it took effect, what gates were evaluated, and why the system promoted/aborted.
2. **Tamper-evident audit trail** suitable for regulated customers’ change-management expectations.
3. **Low risk of sensitive data leakage** (no prompts, user content, or secrets).
4. **Consistent eventing across entry points** (Console, API, automated policy engine actions).

## Non-goals
- Provide a general-purpose eventing framework for all Redwood features.
- Store raw metrics time series in audit logs (we link to evidence queries and dashboards instead).

## Definitions
- **Dedicated pool**: Reserved GPU capacity pool associated with a customer account.
- **Rollout plan**: A staged plan applied to a Dedicated pool.
- **Stage**: A defined traffic/replica partition in the rollout.
- **Gate**: A set of criteria that must pass to promote a stage.
- **Actor**: The entity that initiated the action (human user, service principal, or system automation).
